eastern-dedicated-freight-corridor.confidence_note: Indian courts and tribunals record the project's land takings and several of the card's grievances from outside the lender, on the stretch the Comptroller and Auditor General says the Bank financed (Ludhiana-Khurja-Kanpur-Mughalsarai, 1,183 km, CAG Report No. 48 of 2015). The Central Administrative Tribunal at Allahabad recorded on 3 April 2012 that no decision had been taken on the job-in-lieu-of-land representation of 16 land losers of village Matkutta, Tehsil Sakaldeeh, Chandauli, filed on 3 September 2011. The Allahabad High Court recorded on 10 February 2025 that compensation on a Chandauli award of 1 June 2023 was still unreleased pending an enquiry into shares, and on 14 March 2024 quashed an order recovering part of the compensation already paid to two Chandauli landholders because the inquiries behind it were ex parte. On 12 December 2022 the same court recorded that land at village Kalna Gaharwar, Mirzapur had neither been acquired nor sold to the corridor while construction was at the verge of completion, and said entry on it without due process would be unlawful. What no outside document carries is the card's central claims: the 85,000 project-affected people, the count of families paid at pre-2013 rates, and the unrest and protest claims. One case was dismissed with costs for concealment (Ram Kishun, 18 March 2021), which cuts the other way.

field_changes.community: Across the three loans, nearly 85,000 people in about 1,000 villages in four states were affected by land acquisition (4,336 hectares). The World Bank reports many complaints from people paid lower rates used before India's 2013 land law raised compensation, and unrest over unpaid or late compensation that disrupted construction in some places. Some families went to court seeking the better terms given to 265 neighbouring households. In Chandauli, farmers in Cheeto village held a sit-in from 25 February 2016, and CPI (ML) Liberation workers began a hunger strike on 11 July 2016. They said promised jobs, market-price compensation and rehabilitation were not given. Indian court and tribunal records from the same districts show what the disputes looked like. Sixteen land losers of village Matkutta, Tehsil Sakaldeeh, Chandauli asked the Central Administrative Tribunal at Allahabad for the job the Railway Board's policy of 16 July 2010 promised people who lost land; the tribunal recorded on 3 April 2012 that their representation of 3 September 2011 had not been decided, and gave the Railways two months to decide it. In village Akbarpur, Tehsil Sakaldiha, Chandauli, the award of 11 March 2013 priced seven houses standing on one plot, gata 99, at between 40,800 and 832,200 rupees (Allahabad High Court, 18 March 2021, a petition the court dismissed with 20,000 rupees in costs for concealing that the family had been paid). At village Dharna in the same district the High Court recorded on 10 February 2025 that compensation under an award of 1 June 2023 had still not been released while an enquiry into shares went on. In Mirzapur the High Court recorded on 12 December 2022 that land at village Kalna Gaharwar had neither been acquired nor sold to the corridor, and said it would be unlawful for the Railways to enter it without due process; the owners said the authorities had begun demolition without paying. In Gautam Budh Nagar, where the corridor was built with government money after the Bank dropped the Khurja-Dadri stretch, the High Court held on 27 August 2021 that landholders of villages Chamrawali-Boraki, Rithauri and Hazratpur had filed objections in time, that the objections were never heard or decided, and that the competent authority told the Ministry of Railways on 24 September 2019 that no objections had been filed; it refused to quash the acquisition because the line was nearly finished, ordered compensation at current market rates, and asked the Chief Secretary of Uttar Pradesh to hold an inquiry into the false report. In Bihar the Patna High Court set aside on 27 June 2014 the compensation orders the Commissioner-cum-Arbitrator had passed for more than thirty landholders of village Barej, Mohania, Kaimur without notice or hearing, and sent them back to be heard.

corrections: The card calls the project 'Uttar Pradesh, India' and places the harm in that state; the Comptroller and Auditor General's Report No. 48 of 2015 (chapter 3) states that the World Bank agreed in May 2011 to fund only the Ludhiana-Khurja-Kanpur-Mughalsarai stretch of 1,183 km, and the court records of corridor land disputes sit in Gautam Budh Nagar, Chandauli and Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh and in Kaimur in Bihar. The Kaimur cases are on the Mughalsarai-Sonnagar section, which that CAG chapter lists separately from the Bank-funded stretch, so they are corridor harm but probably not Bank-funded corridor harm; the Gautam Budh Nagar cases are on the Dadri spur, which the card itself says the Bank dropped.

The card's outcome field reports the lender's finding that no land acquisition issues were pending at closing. Allahabad High Court orders of 14 March 2024, 10 February 2025 and 8 April 2025 and a Patna High Court order of 27 June 2014 show compensation, apportionment and rehabilitation claims on corridor land still unresolved in court well after the loans closed, including an award of 1 June 2023 whose money had not been released by February 2025.
eastern-dedicated-freight-corridor.what_the_outside_source_settles: That land and houses were taken for this corridor from named families in named villages of Chandauli and Mirzapur, with dates and awarded sums; that the Railway Board's job-in-lieu-of-land policy generated claims from Chandauli land losers that went undecided, which is the jobs grievance the card attributes to protesters and to a political party; that compensation on corridor land in Chandauli was still unreleased in 2025 and had been clawed back ex parte in one case; that in Gautam Budh Nagar the competent authority reported to the Ministry of Railways that no objections had been filed when objections had been filed, and a High Court ordered an inquiry into who did it; and that in Kaimur an arbitrator fixed compensation for more than thirty landholders without hearing them.
eastern-dedicated-freight-corridor.what_it_does_not_settle: None of the card's quantities. No outside document counts the 85,000 project-affected people, the 4,336 hectares, the families paid at pre-2013 rates, or the 265 neighbouring households said to have had better terms; nor does any outside document reach the Cheeto village sit-in of February 2016 or the July 2016 hunger strike, which remain a wire report of a party's claims. Nothing opened ties a death to the works. And the two judgments with the clearest findings of wrongdoing - Gautam Budh Nagar and Kaimur - are on stretches the CAG chapter and the card itself place outside the Bank's 1,183 km.

nagapattinam-canal-demolition-tsunami-re.confidence_note: The demolition without compensation is stated plainly in the Bank's completion report, which was opened for this round and says at paragraph 53 that the local authorities demolished the affected structures without offering compensation and assistance, and names the North Buckingham canal and Nagapattinam district. It is repeated in the Independent Evaluation Group's review. Both are the lender's own documents and neither names the stretch of canal or the village. Indian Kanoon holds no judgment that pairs a Buckingham canal with Nagapattinam, and nothing on this demolition was found in the index or on the web; no Indian court record, state audit or press report of it was found. One unrelated harm on the same project in the same district is on the court record: 46 or more beneficiaries of village Periyakuthagai, Vedaranyam taluk, Nagapattinam asked the Madras High Court in 2012 to order the completion of the reinforced-concrete-roof houses of package 22 under the project and 500 rupees a month until handover, and the petition sat for ten years and was dismissed for non-prosecution on 13 October 2022. That is a different set of people and different works, so it does not move the card. The completion report also does not say whether the sixth family was ever paid.

lucknow-muzaffarpur-highway-land.confidence_note: Allahabad High Court records carry the harm, name the works and match the dates. The widening of National Highway 28 from kilometre 9 to kilometre 360.57, Lucknow to the Uttar Pradesh-Bihar border, began with a notification under section 3A of the National Highways Act 1956 dated 26 May 2004; the Special Land Acquisition Officer at Barabanki valued the land as agricultural and made awards on 7 December 2005 and 31 August 2006. In the case of Ram Awadh of village Malinpur, Tehsil Ramsanehighat, Barabanki, the award of 31 August 2006 priced his land at 4.20 rupees a square foot; the District Magistrate of Barabanki, sitting as arbitrator, raised it on 18 September 2015 to 52 rupees a square foot with 9 per cent interest from the date of possession, and on 16 April 2019 the High Court recorded that the National Highways Authority had not deposited the enhanced sum and dismissed his petition, because the Authority's challenge to the award was still pending. For nine other Barabanki landholders an arbitral award of 20 May 2015 found their land should have been valued at non-agricultural rates, at 490 rupees a square metre after a 30 per cent deduction, with 9 per cent interest from the date of acquisition; the Authority's objections were dismissed by the Additional District Judge, and its appeals were held time-barred on 31 October 2023. At Basti, Savitri Devi's plot 294 (renumbered 323) of 0.038 hectare with the house on it was acquired for the same highway; on 5 July 2024 the High Court set aside the part of the arbitral award of 11 December 2008 that dealt with the land and sent it back to be recalculated. The counts on the card - 442 hectares, 14,976 titleholders and 8,418 people without title - remain the lender's own and are not corroborated anywhere outside it.

field_changes.community: The Bank's completion report describes the project's displacement and resettlement impacts as 'high in magnitude as well as intensity' and counts the taking of 442 hectares of private land from about 14,976 titleholders and 8,418 people without title, and 259 religious properties. It says that by the closing date land acquisition and resettlement were fully completed and all affected families had received their compensation and main entitlements, except a few whose cases were in court over who owned the land. Court records of the same works tell a different story about what was in court. The land was taken under section 3A of the National Highways Act 1956 by a notification of 26 May 2004 covering kilometre 9 to kilometre 360.57, Lucknow to the Uttar Pradesh-Bihar border, and the Special Land Acquisition Officer at Barabanki valued it as agricultural land. Ram Awadh of village Malinpur, Tehsil Ramsanehighat, Barabanki was awarded 4.20 rupees a square foot on 31 August 2006; the District Magistrate of Barabanki, sitting as arbitrator under section 3G(5), raised that to 52 rupees a square foot with 9 per cent interest on 18 September 2015, and on 16 April 2019 the Allahabad High Court recorded that the National Highways Authority had still not deposited the enhanced amount and dismissed his petition for it, because the Authority's own challenge to the award was pending and the rules barred payment until it was decided. Nine Barabanki landholders whose award was made on 7 December 2005 won an arbitral award on 20 May 2015 holding that land within 100 metres of the highway should have been paid for at non-agricultural rates, 490 rupees a square metre after a 30 per cent deduction, with 9 per cent interest from the date of acquisition; the Authority's objection was dismissed by the Additional District Judge at Barabanki and its appeals were held time-barred on 31 October 2023, eighteen years after the award. At Basti, Savitri Devi's plot of 0.038 hectare and the house on it were acquired for the same highway, and on 5 July 2024 the High Court set aside the land part of the arbitral award of 11 December 2008 as patently illegal and sent it back to the arbitrator to be recalculated. Four religious properties could not be moved because religious leaders took hard positions. Stretches of land totalling up to 1,800 metres were taken out of the project because ownership disputes took too long to settle; the highways authority said it would do that work with its own money. Over the life of the project the Bank's own ratings for resettlement implementation moved from satisfactory to unsatisfactory and back to satisfactory. The consultants who were to evaluate what happened to resettled people at the end of the project were not hired until the closing date, so that evaluation was still under way; the Independent Evaluation Group says the Bank would keep monitoring it until the final report was submitted. The Independent Evaluation Group notes that the completion report does not state that all safeguards were met or complied with. At stakeholder workshops the general view reported was that land acquisition and resettlement 'was done reasonably well except for a few stray cases of dissatisfaction', and that landowners along the road were pleased because their asset values had risen; many people at the same workshops said road safety had worsened because of higher speeds.

corrections: The card repeats the completion report's statement that by the closing date all affected families had received their compensation and main entitlements, except a few whose cases were in court over who owned the land. The cases on the Allahabad High Court's record are not about who owned the land. They are about how much the land was worth: landowners at Barabanki and Basti were paid at agricultural or disputed rates, arbitrators appointed under section 3G(5) of the National Highways Act found the rates too low, and the National Highways Authority of India then litigated against paying the enhanced amounts until 2019, 2023 and 2024 - seven to twelve years after the loan closed on 30 June 2012.

The card's confidence note says no press report, court record or NGO field research on this corridor's resettlement was found. Three Allahabad High Court judgments on the corridor's compensation exist and are cited above; the note should be replaced.
lucknow-muzaffarpur-highway-land.what_the_outside_source_settles: That the takings on this card happened, under which law and on what dates, in which districts, and that compensation on at least part of the corridor was first fixed at agricultural rates and then found by the state's own arbitrators to be too low. It also settles that payment of the corrected amounts was not complete when the loan closed and was still being fought in 2023 and 2024, with named parties, named villages and plot numbers, and case numbers.
lucknow-muzaffarpur-highway-land.what_it_does_not_settle: The scale. The judgments cover one landowner at Malinpur, nine at Barabanki and one at Basti; nothing outside the lender counts the 442 hectares, the 14,976 titleholders or the 8,418 people without title, and nothing supports the ICIJ figure of 75,434. Nor do they say anything about the 259 religious properties, about anybody losing a home as against part of a field, or about what happened to people without title, who cannot bring an arbitration over the value of land they do not own. No outside source was found for the end-of-project assessment of resettled people that the Bank never completed.

dehlon-bypass-uncompensated-landowner.confidence_note: The Dehlon sequence, the two fatal accidents and the blocked entrances all come from the Independent Evaluation Group's review of the Bank's completion report, which cites that report paragraph by paragraph; the completion report itself is not disclosed. Indian Kanoon holds no judgment on the Dehlon plot. The High Court case the review describes - filed in May 2017 by a co-owner who refused the compensation offered, heard on 31 January 2018 without the plaintiff appearing - was searched for by the bypass name, by the project name and by the implementing board's name and does not appear in the index; Punjab and Haryana High Court orders of this kind are often not reported there. What the index does hold are two Income Tax Appellate Tribunal orders on the concessionaire that operates the road, which record that the Punjab Roads and Bridges Development Board developed the 71.352 km Ludhiana-Malerkotla-Sangrur road under World Bank aid and that the Dehlon bypass runs 2.98 km from kilometre 18+750 to kilometre 20+800; they say nothing about any plot, owner or payment. A High Court judgment of 6 June 2016 on the project's tendering confirms the Bank loan from outside the lender but concerns which contractor was eligible to bid. The Board's own website lists the bypass's acquisition papers under the 2013 land law, including a second unclaimed-compensation notice and an announcement of award; the notice, read through a fetch tool, is undated and names no project, so it cannot be tied to this plot or these dates. Nobody is named except by role, the drains that blocked 'numerous' entrances are not counted, and the two deaths are recorded in one sentence with no detail at all.
